**Witness:** 12/010–016; “enveloppe algébrique”; \(\varepsilon\gamma(\lambda)=\lambda^2\). **Kind:** own idea. **Confidence:** medium as a comparison method, because the pages give linear realizations but no recognition theorem for the full profinite subgroup.

**Witness:** 12/016–019; “conjuguées complexes”; “Structures de positivité”. **Kind:** own idea. **Confidence:** high for the linear-algebra distinction, not asserted as a counterexample motive.

At the level of linear algebra, the real form with matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) is preserved by ordinary complex conjugation but is indefinite. **Witness:** 12/005 and 012–016; “(pro)réductif”; “centre”; “central”. **Kind:** own idea. **Confidence:** high for the distinction, because a torus is an immediate test case.

### Q01 — Is the category built from cote 16’s Lefschetz correspondence rings?

**Kind:** unpursued implication. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 056 and059, “anneau des correspondances” and “la catégorie des motifs”; CT16/018 and049, “anneau … de correspondances Lefschetzien” and “category of motives which is semi-simple”. **Context search:** catégorie; correspondances; Lefschetz; projecteurs; enveloppe. **Context:** CN S3, S13–S16 and HU’s later “L’enveloppe pseudo-abélienne” / “L’exemple des variétés”, pp.143–151, outside this packet. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; MPL_11_043-058+56 N031; MPL_14_087-132 M01; MPL_15_087-138 L01; MPL_60_002-035 C01.

**The current pages use a category of motives; they do not construct it from the single Lefschetz operator-ring formalism.** A correspondence construction needs morphisms between varieties, an equivalence relation on cycles, projectors, tensor products, and Tate twists; the classical objects \((X,p,m)\) are described in [J92, pp.447–448]. CT16’s rings supply compatible operator and decomposition data, while HU locates a broader categorical construction on later, unsupplied leaves. The precise addition here is the Galois-commutant formulation on scan 056 and the proposed tensor-categorical Lie pro-motive on scan 059.

### Q03 — Is the Lefschetz grading the weight cocharacter?

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 056 and086, “poids 0” and “purs de poids \(\rho\)”; CT16/016–017, the grading projectors. **Context search:** poids; graduation; central; \(\pi_i\); cocaractère. **Context:** HU “Structures supplémentaires sur le groupe de Galois motivique”, pp.14–16, outside the packet, gives a central weight cocharacter and \(\varepsilon(y(\lambda))=\lambda^2\). **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; MPL_15_087-138 L07/§111.

**The two gradings should not be identified:** a tensor-compatible grading of objects gives a central cocharacter [DM22, Definition 5.1], whereas the usual Lefschetz Cartan acts on \(H^i(X)\) by \(i-\dim X\) and satisfies \([h,L]=2L\). A nontrivial image of that Cartan cannot simultaneously be the central weight operator in the same Lie algebra. **Confidence: high under these standard conventions**, because centrality contradicts the nonzero bracket; this is a structural comparison, not a claim that the present pages contain the cocharacter formula.

### N010 — What the double-commutant argument actually establishes

**Kind:** unproved claim. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 056, “Le deuxième énoncé + injectivité … entraîne tout”. **Context search:** commutant; semi-simple; Hodge; correspondances. **Context:** HU §14 p.55 = scan 056 names the double-commutant theorem; CT16/049 explicitly connects the Hodge index relation with semisimplicity of the correspondence ring. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #7 and #2.

Once the correspondence algebra is finite-dimensional semisimple and acts faithfully, equality of the Galois enveloping algebra with its commutant gives the reverse commutant equality by the semisimple bicommutant theorem. The conditional algebra argument is sound, but the geometric semisimplicity and correspondence identification are precisely substantive hypotheses. Thus the final sentence is a reduction of the desired comparison, not a proof of Tate or of the Hodge standard conjecture.

### N016 — Analytic Lie algebra and algebraic Lie algebra must be distinguished

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 057–059, “l’image” and “le promotif … Z(0)”. **Context search:** corps fini; Lie; pro-motif; Zariski; Frobenius. **Context:** HU §14 p.58 = scan 059 identifies the proposal with a tannakian Lie algebra and also describes a one-dimensional finite-field analytic image; this is an inference gap rather than an established equivalence. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; LM6 A.22.

For \(\ell\ne5\), let \(F=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-5\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\): its compact procyclic closure in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbf Z_\ell)\) has analytic Lie dimension one, whereas its eigenvalues, roots of \(t^2-t+5\), are multiplicatively independent and its algebraic closure is a two-dimensional torus. Independence follows from their coprime principal ideals of norm five, since their sum is one; the analytic dimension is one because the closure is infinite and topologically generated by one element. **Confidence: high for this distinction**, which prevents the finite-field sentence from identifying the full motivic Galois group with \(\mathbf G_m\), but does not decide whether the author intended an analytic or an algebraic Lie object throughout.

For a homomorphism from the procyclic Galois group normalized to take Frobenius to one, restriction to the degree-\(n\) subgroup multiplies that value by \(n\). The inverse identification of a cohomology class with a scalar may therefore acquire \(1/n\), depending on which map is being compared. This explains why the direction must be specified and why HU’s reciprocal should not replace the frozen multiplier.

### N033 — The expected rational-point formula contains a finiteness conjecture

**Kind:** conjecture. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 075, “raisons heuristiques convaincantes” and the boxed finiteness of \(H^1(S,A)(\ell)\). **Context search:** Kummer; fini; Mordell; Lang; \(H^1(S,A)\). **Context:** HU §16 pp.73–79 = scans 074–080 follows the same chain; CT16/021, equations (8.3)–(8.7), and023, equations (8.8)–(8.9), supply direct reused Kummer/Picard/Brauer context, while CT44/004–005 concerns heights rather than this general finiteness. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #12; SECTIONS_OVER_Q A.182/A.186/A.187/A.188; FERMAT_SUCCESSOR A.53/A.54.

Kummer theory gives a rationalized exact sequence whose outer terms are \(A(S)\otimes\mathbf Q_\ell\) and the rational Tate module of \(H^1(S,A)\), so the desired formula requires the latter to vanish. Converting that vanishing into finiteness uses finite-cotype information, not just the displayed equality of vector-space dimensions. The arbitrary finite-type-base conjecture should not be treated as established by the special Jacobian computations claimed in RS, or by Lang’s theorem for \(S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q\).

### N035 — The discrete lattice cohomology formula needs its quotient

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 076 and079, “\((\underline M\otimes Q/Z)^\pi\)” and “coh. galoisienne de \(\widehat Z\)”. **Context search:** \(H^1\); \(M\); quotient; fini; galoisienne. **Context:** HU §16 pp.75–78 = scans 076–079 already qualifies the invariants formula by a quotient; the precise role of the underlined \(M\) remains a notation question. **RS:** WG2 §3.2 #7; no direct RS result.

For an ordinary torsion-free finitely generated discrete \(\pi\)-module, the long exact sequence of \(0\to M\to M\otimes\mathbf Q\to M\otimes\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z\to0\) identifies \(H^1(\pi,M)\) with the quotient of \((M\otimes\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z)^\pi\) by the image of \((M\otimes\mathbf Q)^\pi\). The trivial module \(M=\mathbf Z\) makes the issue immediate: continuous \(H^1(\widehat{\mathbf Z},\mathbf Z)=0\), while \((\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z)^\pi=\mathbf Q/\mathbf Z\). **Confidence: high for this check**, which corroborates HU’s qualification without deciding whether an earlier definition of the underlining already includes the quotient.

### N040 — “Essentially BSD” is a rank assertion with qualifications

**Kind:** conjecture. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 080, “essentiellement équivalente à la conjecture de Birch–Swinnerton Dyer”. **Context search:** Birch; Swinnerton; rang; invariants; Tate. **Context:** HU §16 p.79 = scan 080 identifies the same rank comparison; CT44/004–005 supplies the height/polarization programme. **RS:** WG H9; SECTIONS_OVER_Q A.182/A.186/A.187/A.188; FERMAT_SUCCESSOR A.53.

The displayed equality compares the Mordell–Weil rank with a Frobenius-invariant cohomological rank, so the immediate target is the rank/Tate–Shafarevich side of BSD in the appropriate function-field setting. It does not itself contain the full leading-coefficient formula with regulator, periods, Tamagawa factors, and torsion. The word “essentiellement” should remain in any account of this connection. For an abelian variety over a global function field, Kato–Trihan proves the full BSD conjectures assuming finiteness of one \(\ell\)-primary part of Sha [KT03, opening theorem]; this modern bridge has field and local-condition hypotheses not stated for every base here.

**Kind:** unproved claim. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 082, “essentiellement un p-groupe, modulo groupe fini !”. **Context search:** local; Tate; dual; \(K_x\); p-groupe. **Context:** HU p.81 = scan 082 abbreviates the quotation but explicitly restores the finite-error and prime-to-\(p\) qualifications in its full footnote; CT16/028 and030 cite and discuss earlier Tate local-cohomology work. **RS:** FLAGGED_149 B9; FERMAT_SUCCESSOR A.54; LM7 E.23.

The local duality comparison with \(A^*(K_x)\) separates the finite prime-to-\(p\) contribution from potentially much larger \(p\)-primary information; it does not say the whole local group is finite [ML70/72]. The asserted isomorphism for the punctured curve relied on the problematic global vanishings, but a finite prime-to-\(p\) conclusion may still follow from the localization sequence and global finiteness without that isomorphism. This is a useful analogy with RS’s prime-to-\(p\)/\(p\)-primary boundary, not a solution of its anabelian point or section questions.

### N043 — The \(\mathbf G_m\) calculation separates units, Picard, and Brauer data

**Kind:** unproved claim. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 084, “coBrauer” and “Calculs pour … Q_l(1)”. **Context search:** Kummer; Picard; Brauer; unités; \(G_m\). **Context:** HU “Calculs sur Q_l(1) et G_m”, p.83 = scan 084, rewrites the degree-one and degree-two calculations; CT16/021, equations (8.3)–(8.7), and023, equations (8.8)–(8.9), provide direct reused Kummer/Picard/Brauer context. **RS:** WG2 §3.2 #7; MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 M07.

The étale Kummer sequence is exact on every scheme where \(\ell\) is invertible; after the required inverse-limit and finiteness arguments, degree one involves units and degree two involves Picard data plus the rational Tate module of the cohomological Brauer group. Those are separate pieces and do not imply the displayed high-degree vanishing. The literal scope “X de type fini sur Z” does not ensure invertibility of \(\ell\); regularity, where needed for subsequent identifications or residue formulas, is an additional hypothesis of those steps rather than of Kummer exactness itself.

### N044 — Puncturing a proper curve has a residue-count correction

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 084, “faux quand on lui enlève des pts” and “le rang … augmente d’autant”. **Context search:** Brauer; points; ouvert; résidus; Artin. **Context:** HU p.83 = scan 084 makes the same proper/open comparison without a complete residue count; CT16/021 and023 supply related Brauer/Tate-module context, without this residue count. **RS:** LM7 C.1/C.5; MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 B04.

For a smooth proper geometrically connected curve over a finite field with \(r\ge1\) rational points removed, the Brauer residue terms satisfy one global sum relation, so their \(\ell\)-corank is \(r-1\), not \(r\). In particular one rational puncture does not force an infinite Brauer group, whereas \(\mathbf P^1-\{0,\infty\}\) provides the familiar nonproper contribution. **Confidence: high under these stated curve hypotheses**, by the residue sequence [ADT, II.2.1], and the formula is a research qualification of the page’s terse count, not a correction of its uncertain index.

### N045 — A singular proper example answers the unrestricted \(i\ge4\) question negatively

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 084, “Hⁱ(X,Q_l(1))=0 … si i≥4 ??”. **Context search:** \(i\ge4\); singulier; poids zéro; \(G_m\); dual complex. **Context:** HU p.83 = scan 084 leaves this question open; CT16/047 asks for singular-variety reformulations but contains no such example. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; WG2 §3.2 #7; no direct RS result.

Let \(D=\{x_0x_1x_2x_3=0\}\subset\mathbf P^3_{\mathbf F_q}\) and \(X=D\times\mathbf P^1\), with \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}\mathbf F_q\): the exact alternating complex of the four planes, six lines, and four triple points has a Frobenius-fixed weight-zero \(H^2\) equal to the top cohomology of the tetrahedron boundary. More explicitly, the strata calculation gives \(H^2(\overline D)=\mathbf Q_\ell\oplus\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)\), \(H^3(\overline D)=\mathbf Q_\ell(-1)^3\), and \(H^4(\overline D)=\mathbf Q_\ell(-2)^4\), so Künneth and Hochschild–Serre give \(\dim H^4(X,\mathbf Q_\ell(1))=3+1=4\). The detailed stalk-exactness and spectral-sequence check is retained in the arithmetic support record, and this example addresses the literal finite-type scope, without contradicting the smooth finite-field vanishing consequence of [D80, Corollary 3.3.5]. **Confidence: high**, from the finite incidence-complex calculation; it is an explicit standard-method counterexample supplied here, with no claim of novelty.

**Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scan 087, “un cône convexe fermé” and “un intérieur non vide”. **Context search:** cône; intérieur; pseudo-ample; réel. **Context:** HU §17 p.86 = scan 087 repeats the cone axioms; CT16/025–027 discusses Hodge-type positivity in another formalism. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 B03.

Because \(\Phi^s(M)\) is first declared a rational vector space, an interpretation should specify whether “closed” and “interior” are taken after tensoring with \(\mathbf R\) or in the induced topology on rational points. The usual real cone of positive semidefinite forms supplies a model, with positive definite forms as its interior, but does not itself construct the required motivic cone. **Confidence: high in the need to specify topology**, because the two ambient spaces and their rational-point sets are distinct objects.

Over a field, finite dimension over \(k\) gives the finite-length \(k[t]\)-module framework used in the argument, but over a general ring finite projectivity is a different condition. The identity matrix and the nontrivial unipotent matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) have the same determinant \(\det(1-tF)=(1-t)^2\) and all the same power traces, but define nonisomorphic Frobenius modules. ### N058 — The birational truncation discards lower-dimensional contributions

**Kind:** unproved claim. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 093–094, “poids ≤2n−2+\(\rho\)” and “invariant birationnel”. **Context search:** ouvert; dimension; poids; niveau; birationnel. **Context:** HU §18 pp.92–93 = scans 093–094 relates this to §12 pp.42–51; the direct current overlap is scan 052. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3; MPL_15_087-138 §123.

The intended mechanism is localization: the difference between a variety and a dense open lies on a set of dimension at most \(n-1\), whose compactly supported \(L\)-factor lies below the proposed cutoff. This explains why the top contribution is birational, while the finer level filtration is needed for stronger invariants. **Kind:** own idea. **Witness:** 12.pdf, scans 051 and073, “si M pur de poids \(\rho\)” and the “sauf si” inequalities. **Context search:** constant tordu; lisse; poids; \(R^1\); Legendre. **Context:** HU’s “Motifs constants tordus”, pp.35–40, outside the packet, allows lisse realizations, while HU p.50/p.72 = scans 051/073 repeats the tight bound and its later p.107 gives weaker coefficient bounds while leaving proposed stronger improvements open; CT has no corresponding example. **RS:** MPL_14_002-044 B04; WG2 §2.4 #3; no direct RS result.

Take \(U=\mathbf P^1_{\mathbf F_5}-\{0,1,\infty\}\) and the Legendre family \(f:E\to U\), with \(\ell\ne5\) and \(V=R^1f_*\mathbf Q_\ell\) pure of weight one: the explicit trace calculation [ST-L] gives two eigenvalues one on \(H_c^1(\overline U,V)\). Since \(V^\vee\simeq V(1)\), curve duality gives \(H^1(\overline U,V)\simeq H_c^1(\overline U,V)^\vee(-2)\), of weight four, exceeding the asserted \(\rho+2i=3\). More sharply \(M=V(2)\) has weight \(-3\) and \(H^1(\overline U,M)\) has eigenvalue one, hence nonzero invariants and nonzero \(H^1(U,M)\), although both degree-one alternatives on scan 073 fail. **Confidence: high**, from the explicit primary-source computation and duality [ST-D]; the counterexample concerns general pure lisse geometric coefficients under the usual twist convention, while geometrically constant or finite-monodromy coefficients require a separate statement.

### Scope checks that matter to the conclusions

The group comparison [CG17], the numerical semisimplicity theorem [J92], the motivated/pure-Nori comparison [A13], and the descent theorem [K25] concern different categories or functors. Their coexistence does not identify every arithmetic Galois image, prove all classical cycle conjectures, or resolve the manuscript’s absolute-cohomology axioms. The exact numerical period question remains distinct from [BT25]’s functional theorem.

The counterexample in N045 uses a singular scheme. For a smooth separated finite-type \(X/\mathbf F_q\), [D80, Corollary 3.3.5] puts \(H^{i-1}(\overline X,\mathbf Q_\ell(1))\) in weights at least \(i-3\) and \(H^i(\overline X,\mathbf Q_\ell(1))\) in weights at least \(i-2\); for \(i\ge4\), neither has eigenvalue one, and Hochschild–Serre gives \(H^i(X,\mathbf Q_\ell(1))=0\). This is an editorial deduction from the cited lower bound and does not invoke the disputed upper bound for varying coefficients.

Oda’s theorem uses a perfect field and a finite group scheme, Milne’s local theorem uses the local topology and duality, and Kato–Trihan’s theorem requires a global function field and a finite Sha component. Those hypotheses identify the additional inputs needed to compare the prime-to-\(p\) calculations with characteristic-\(p\) arithmetic; they are not additions to P12.

## 10. Verification and limits of this return

The deliverable contains all **39 supplied page files**, in the supplied order, and one combined LaTeX fragment. The combined text is an exact concatenation of those files, with no preamble or external image inclusion. The inventory has **628 elements**, every row marked **yes**: 224 text blocks, 97 displays, 25 diagrams, 16 drawings, 156 deletions, 89 insertions, and 21 margin notes.

The separate doubts apparatus records **289 occurrences of \(\backslash\)unsure and 3 \(\backslash\)illegible spans** (an estimated four words altogether), with the notation table and abbreviation concordance. These are reported uncertainties, not an estimate of the total error rate; absence of a doubt mark does not guarantee a correct reading. The most fragile readings remain densely revised passages, small indices and signs, the cancelled draft faces, and the shorter handwritten additions to reused typescripts.

The research apparatus has **75 principal notes** (Q01–Q11 and N001–N064), the four-row linear/non-linear comparison, **32 self-flag entries**, **9 visible-revision entries**, **5 separate cancellation/contradiction entries**, **9 documentary title entries**, and **24 post-freeze reading questions**. These are 158 identified items, with thematic overlap recorded deliberately rather than counted as 158 independent mathematical results. Each principal note was checked for its witness, kind, context relationship, RS bearing, and the confidence/reason qualification where it is an own idea.

The context-search ledger records literal and normalized searches against the supplied files, with exact source locators and per-source counts; a zero literal hit is not treated as proof of thematic absence. Mathematical support records preserve the finite incidence calculation for N045, the Legendre derivation for N064, and the primary-source scope checks. Independent research review narrowed several context references and theorem hypotheses; it did not revisit or modify the frozen transcription.

Structural validation checks the scan set and order, markers, balanced groups and environments, exact concatenation, inventory schema and completion, and the required files. The 40 frozen SHA-256 hashes (39 pages plus the combined fragment) are verified again at completion, with the result written to progress.log and a verification record. The archive manifest supplies sizes and SHA-256 hashes for its contents and excludes the original attachments, scan images, and copied source/context files.

**No successful LaTeX compilation is claimed.** TeX engine binaries are present, but the environment lacks the LaTeX formats and required classes/packages, including article.cls, amsmath, and tikz-cd; the preserved harness and compile-status record document that limitation. The deliverable is the requested diplomatic LaTeX fragment and supporting apparatus, without a claimed rendered edition.

## 3. Linear statement / non-linear statement

The four pairs are a planning comparison, not four equivalences written in these scans.

| Pair and manuscript anchor | Linear statement | Non-linear statement | Exact scope and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tate / anabelian Hom; 12/142, “pleinement fidèle” | For abelian varieties over a finite field, with l different from the characteristic, `Hom(A,B) ⊗ Z_l → Hom_G(T_l A,T_l B)` is an isomorphism (Tate, 1966, main theorem); over a number field the same result follows from Faltings's endomorphism theorem by applying it to `A × B` (Faltings, 1986, Theorem 4). | For smooth geometrically connected curves `X,Y` over a sub-p-adic field, with `Y` hyperbolic, dominant morphisms correspond to continuous open homomorphisms of arithmetic fundamental groups over the base Galois group, modulo inner conjugation by the geometric target group (Mochizuki, 1999, Theorem A/16.5). | The latter also has a geometrically pro-p version, while its Galois quotient remains the full absolute Galois group; no arbitrary abstract group homomorphisms or section-surjectivity assertion is included. Passing to abelianizations gives a Jacobian map but loses the conditions making a linear map come from a curve map. |
| Semisimplicity / trivial centres; 12/140, “isomotif semi-simple”; 12/114, “semi-simplicité utilisée!” | In characteristic zero, semisimplicity of a neutral Tannakian category corresponds to pro-reductivity of the identity component of its group (Deligne & Milne, 1982/2012, Proposition 2.23 and its extension to the identity component). | The geometric profinite fundamental group of a characteristic-zero hyperbolic curve is centre-free, as are its open subgroups, since these correspond to hyperbolic finite covers (Tamagawa, 1997, Proposition 1.11). | Reductivity allows a central torus: the Tate category has group `G_m`; centre-freeness instead makes the conjugation map `Δ → Aut(Δ)` injective and identifies `Δ` with `Inn(Δ)`. |
| Polarizations / real structures; 12/141, the weight-one abelian-scheme functor; CT 44/2, “polarisation” | A weight-n polarization has the appropriate parity, alternating in odd weight and symmetric in even weight, with positivity after the Weil-operator convention; it is not merely a real involution (Deligne & Milne, 1982/2012, Definition 5.12). | For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve `X/R` of genus at least one, conjugacy classes of sections of `π₁(X) → Gal(C/R)` correspond to connected components of `X(R)` (Stix, 2008, Theorem 26). | The real theorem recovers a finite set of components, not individual real points, and a polarization on `H¹(X(C))` does not supply a section of the arithmetic extension. |
| Weights / cyclotomic normalizers; 12/115, “poids entre”; 12/141, “le poids” | At a good finite place of residue characteristic different from l, the eigenvalues of arithmetic Frobenius on `V_l J` have absolute value `q^(1/2)`, while its value on `Q_l(1)` is `q`; hence `Hom_G(Q_l(1),V_l J)=0` after any finite extension with such a place (Serre & Tate, 1968, Theorem 3). | For affine hyperbolic curves over finitely generated fields of characteristic zero, the cyclotomic-normalizer characterization of cusp inertia is substantially stronger than an open image for the normalizer alone; Tamagawa (1997, §7C) states Nakamura's result with the actual cyclotomic action condition. | The weight test excludes nonzero cyclotomic images in a Jacobian quotient; to classify a subgroup invisible there requires finite-cover detection and control of the conjugation character, precisely the extra issues reflected by RS LM6 A.22 and A.50. |

### LN02 — A concrete gap between Jacobian Hom and curve Hom

**Witness/kind:** 12/142, “pleinement fidèle”; own idea. **Confidence/reason:** high, because Riemann–Hurwitz and the action on a polarization give an elementary test. **Context search:** `Tate|Hom|fidèle` → CT 44/8 and RS `MPL_18_018-062 §3`; this **adds** a scope example to the supplied analogy, without changing either status. **Bears on:** `MPL_18_018-062 §3`, first-pass lead.

For a smooth proper curve `X` of genus at least two over a number field, multiplication by two on `J_X` supplies an integral Galois-equivariant endomorphism of `T_l J_X`, but cannot be induced by a dominant self-map of `X`. Indeed, Riemann–Hurwitz makes every such self-map an automorphism, whose map on `H¹` preserves the canonical symplectic form, whereas multiplication by two scales it by four. This elementary example explains why abelianization does not turn the anabelian Hom statement into the linear one.

### SM14 — Those examples satisfy the manuscript's all-prime nonramification condition

**Witness/kind:** 12/142, lines 14–17, interpreted with 12/140; own idea. **Quotation:** “∀l … non ramifié sur S_l.” **Confidence/reason:** high, because the deduction uses purity for finite étale covers and the literal open subset `S[1/p]`. **Context search:** `non ramifié|dim 2|image inverse` → Hua XIII; no CT counterexample; this **adds** the exact comparison that Hua leaves open. **Bears on:** WG2 §2.4 #3 and WG2 §3.2 #7, unchecked plans.

Let `A_U` be one of the nonextendible examples of SM13, where `U=S\{m}` and `S=Spec R`; for every l different from p its finite étale torsion covers on U extend uniquely to S by regular-local purity (Stacks Project, Tag 0BMA(1)). For l=p, the required open subset `S[1/p]` lies in U, where the abelian scheme already exists, so its p-adic representation is unramified relative to that open. Hence the generic abelian variety meets all the manuscript's l-adic conditions but cannot extend to S, since an extension would restrict to the unique model `A_U`. This deduction answers the unrestricted sufficiency question, and does not claim a new counterexample beyond the cited literature.

### SM18 — The reduction to a prime index still needs proof

**Witness/kind:** 12/142, lines 25–26; unproved claim. **Quotation:** “il y en aurait aussi avec un indice premier.” **Context search:** `indice premier|sous-groupe fini|plat` → Hua XIII omits this reduction; CT 16/56 discusses finite étale algebras but does not give this subgroup reduction. **Relation:** the frozen page **adds** an unproved strengthening beyond Hua's summary. **Bears on:** WG2 §2.4 #3, unchecked plan.

A reduction from a finite generic subgroup to a prime-order step must preserve the base hypotheses and the failure of flat extension, rather than merely factor the order of the group over an algebraic closure. In particular, a finite Galois module need not have a Galois-stable subgroup of prime order, and a field extension that creates such a subgroup can change the regularity or ramification of the base model. ### M03 — Why deleting a separate Hom-finiteness hypothesis is harmless here

**Witness:** cote 12, scan 145, lines 14–18. **Kind:** unpursued implication. **Quotation:** deleted “Fl(X,Y) sont des vectoriels de dim finie”; retained “Fl(X,X) ... de dim finie ... semi-simple”. **Context search:** `dimension finie|Hom|semi-simple` → CT 16/049; CN §S14; Hua, “L'enveloppe pseudo-abélienne (pages 143 à 148)”. **Relation:** adds a categorical explanation to CT's one-object endomorphism discussion and supports Hua's final hypothesis list. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #7 and WG2 §2.4 #3 (unchecked plans).

Assuming finite biproducts, Hom(X,Y) is the matrix corner e_Y End(X⊕Y)e_X, so finite-dimensionality of every endomorphism algebra already implies finite-dimensionality of every Hom. The deletion therefore removes a redundant condition under that interpretation of additivity. It does not justify dropping finiteness of endomorphism algebras, which is used again for the chain condition.

The map f ↦ π′fπ identifies the written quotient with π′ Hom(X,X′) π: on the intertwining subspace it has precisely the written kernel, and every corner element already intertwines the projectors. Composition descends because the corner multiplication is ordinary composition with the intervening idempotent. This verifies the local definition without requiring the geometric conjectures discussed in cote 16.

### M06 — Recovering the generalized-inverse argument without assuming abelianness

**Witness:** cote 12, scan 147, inserted v and oval of four identities; scan 148, direct-morphism criterion. **Kind:** unproved claim. **Quotation:** “v∈U”; “πv=v, uπ=u”; “Tout morphisme ... est ‘direct’”. **Context search:** `inverse|semi-simple|left|right` → CT 16/049; CN §S14; Hua, “L'enveloppe pseudo-abélienne (pages 143 à 148)”. **Relation:** adds the algebraic mechanism sought in CT 16/049 and agrees with the substance of Hua's reconstruction. **RS:** WG2 §2.4 #3 (unchecked plan).

For a semisimple finite-dimensional ring U, choose an inner inverse v₀ with uv₀u=u and replace it by v=v₀uv₀, which also satisfies vuv=v. Then π=vu and ϖ=uv are idempotent, u identifies their split images, and their complementary summands give kernel and cokernel objects. This supplies the categorical argument without using the manuscript's intervening phrase about an action “sur un objet d'une catégorie abélienne” as a premise, which would otherwise assume the conclusion.

### M09 — What the finite chain condition actually proves

**Witness:** cote 12, scan 147, final paragraph; scan 148, condition (i). **Kind:** unproved claim. **Quotation:** “conditions de chaînes”; “de dim finie”. **Context search:** `chaînes|finie|semi-simple` → Hua, “L'enveloppe pseudo-abélienne (pages 143 à 148)”; CT 16/049; CN §S14–S15. **Relation:** adds the finite-length part of the categorical argument to CT's ring claim. **RS:** WG2 §2.3 #7 and WG2 §2.4 #3 (unchecked).

A strictly growing chain of direct summands of P produces successively nonzero orthogonal idempotents in End(P), so its length is bounded by dim_Q End(P). Once every morphism has the split normal form, all subobjects are such summands, making the same bound a finite-length bound in the resulting abelian category. The chain argument and the split-morphism argument are both needed for the manuscript's stated finite semisimplicity convention.

A biadditive F extends by F((X,p),(Y,q))=(F(X,Y),F(p,q)); idempotence follows from functoriality. Associativity, symmetry, and unit constraints restrict to these images and inherit their coherence identities, so the essential uniqueness is the same split-idempotent universal property in two variables. **Witness:** cote 12, scans 144–149, scope of the abstract construction; no sl₂ or weight cocharacter appears there. **Kind:** unpursued implication / bounded comparison. **Quotation:** “catégories multiplicatives”; “motifs semi-simples”. **Context search:** `sl₂|Lefschetz|graduation|cocaractère|poids` → CT 16/014 (integral model), 16/015 (matrix units), 16/016 (projector grading), 16/017 (grading requirement), 16/018 (Lefschetz ring), and 16/049 (semisimple motive programme); CN §S2–S6; Hua, “Structures supplémentaires sur le groupe de Galois motivique (pages 14 à 16)”. **Relation:** distinguishes the two structures joined conjecturally by the plan. **RS:** MPL_14_087-132 M04 and MPL_15_087-138 §111 (first-pass leads), MPL_15_087-138 L07 (lead), WG2 §2.3 #2 and WG2 §2.4 #3 (unchecked).

The cited earlier returns already give the projective-line obstruction, so this package does not claim a new counterexample. On H⁰(P¹)⊕H²(P¹), Lefschetz sl₂ has Cartan eigenvalues −1,+1 and raising/lowering maps between the summands, whereas the motivic weight cocharacter has exponents 0,2 and tensor automorphisms preserve the unit summand. The two diagonal actions differ by a scalar shift, and nontrivial sl₂ root operators cannot be the root operators of a central weight cocharacter. Any separate published SL₂ action through correspondences therefore requires its own target and twists; it is not an inclusion of this SL₂ into the Tate motivic Galois group G_m.

### M24 — The Nori–Ayoub theorem is a group comparison, with no automatic cycle conjecture

**Witness:** cote 12, scans 144 and 149, universal additive and monoidal constructions. **Kind:** unpursued implication / literature comparison. **Quotation:** “équivalence de catégories”; “foncteur bi-additif”. **Context search:** `Nori|Ayoub|Galois|Hopf|universel` → RS MPL_18_018-062 MB10, MPL_15_195-228+18_002-017 M07 and S15; Hua, “Motifs sur une base, et le groupe de Galois motivique (pages 5 et 6)”. **Relation:** adds a checked theorem to the earlier lead; differs from a blanket identification with the manuscript's unconstructed category. **RS:** cited entries are first-pass leads, not independently reviewed internal theorems.

Choudhury and Gallauer Alves de Souza (2017, Theorem 9.1) construct inverse Hopf-algebra isomorphisms comparing Nori's and Ayoub's motivic Galois groups; the rational case applies over a field embedded in C with the chosen Betti realization. The theorem does not identify their mixed category with the semisimple category sought on these selected sheets, nor prove Tate, Hodge, or the standard conjectures for algebraic correspondences. It is a precise affirmative answer to one modern group-comparison question, while the geometric identification remains separate.

Oda (1969, Corollary 5.11, p. 131) identifies the Dieudonné module of A[p], for an abelian variety over a perfect field of characteristic p, with H¹_dR(A), including the Hodge subspace through the F and V structure. This answers the filtered-cohomology reconstruction aspect of the question on 54/007 and shows concretely why finite group schemes carry information beyond their abstract geometric points. It does not extend the definition on 12/140 to characteristic p, prove purity over a mixed-characteristic base, or identify the restricted Lie extension on 54/007 without checking conventions.

A characteristic-p enhancement of the proposed integral data should retain the finite flat group scheme or its Dieudonné realization, rather than add only another étale lattice. For a general smooth proper variety Oda's Corollary 5.12 provides a canonical subspace of H¹_dR controlled by p-torsion of the Picard scheme, while the whole-space isomorphism is special to the abelian case. Thus the useful research test is compatibility with this inclusion and its Hodge filtration, not a universal assertion that A[p]-style data reconstruct all first de Rham cohomology.
